docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
KOR-ee, from the greek Κόρη, the queen of the underworld, daughter of Zeus and Demeter. Kore is a numerical tool to study the core flow within rapidly rotating planets or other rotating fluids contained within near-spherical boundaries. The current version solves the linear Navier-Stokes and induction equations for a viscous, incompressible and conductive fluid with an externally imposed magnetic field, and enclosed within a rotating spherical shell.

On the anelastic_log branch, kore solves the linear anelastic equations of a rotating fluid whose density varies with radius, with an entropy equation and without the magnetic field, in a spherical shell or a full sphere (Anelastic equations). Installation and Getting started show how to install it and run a first case.

Kore assumes all dynamical variables to oscillate in a harmonic fashion. The oscillation frequency can be imposed externally, as is the case when doing forced motion studies (e.g. tidal forcing), or it can be obtained as part of the solution to an eigenvalue problem. In Kore's current implementation, the eigenmodes are the inertial modes of the rotating fluid. Inertial modes are the global modes of a rotating flow in which the Coriolis force participates prominently in the restoring force balance.

Kore's distinctive feature is the use of a very efficient spectral method employing Gegenbauer (also known as ultraspherical) polynomials as a basis in the radial direction. This approach leads to sparse matrices representing the differential equations, as opposed to dense matrices, as in traditional Chebyshev colocation methods. Sparse matrices have smaller memory-footprint and are more suitable for systematic core flow studies at extremely low viscosities (or small Ekman numbers).

Kore is free for everyone to use, with no restrictions. Too often in the scientific literature the numerical methods used are presented with enough detail to guarantee reproducibility, but only in principle. Without access to the actual implementation of those methods, which would require a significant amount of work and time to develop, readers are left effectively without the possibility to reproduce or verify the results presented. This leads to very slow scientific progress. We share our code to avoid this.

If this code is useful for your research, we invite you to cite the relevant papers (coming soon) and hope that you can also contribute to the project.

docs.title: Anelastic equations
docs.text: kore solves the linear anelastic equations in the form of Lantz (1992) and Braginsky & Roberts (1995), "LBR", for small perturbations of a background whose density varies with radius. This page gives those equations, what the approximation drops, how kore makes them dimensionless, and where they hold. The Boussinesq equations are a special case. How the code discretizes the equations is on Numerical method, and the terms that a differential rotation adds are derived on Differential rotation.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The background is at rest in the frame rotating at \(\Omega\), spherically symmetric and hydrostatic: density \(\rho_0(r)\), pressure \(p_0(r)\), temperature \(T_0(r)\), gravity \(-g(r)\thinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\) with \(dp_0/dr = -\rho_0 g\), and specific entropy \(s_0(r)\). Its entropy gradient sets the buoyancy frequency,

\[ N^2 = \frac{g\thinspace \alpha T_0}{c_p}\frac{ds_0}{dr}, \]

with \(\alpha\) the thermal expansion coefficient and \(c_p\) the specific heat at constant pressure. The kinematic viscosity \(\nu(r)\) and the thermal diffusivity \(\kappa(r)\) are radial profiles. Background model explains how to choose all of these.

docs.title: The equations
docs.text:
For a perturbation with velocity \(\mathbf u\) and specific entropy \(s'\), the linear LBR equations are

\[ abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf u) = 0, \] \[ \partial_t\mathbf u + 2 hinspace\mathbf\Omega imes\mathbf u = - abla\Pi + g hinspace rac{\alpha T_0 s'}{c_p} hinspace\hat{\mathbf r} + rac{1}{ ho_0} abla\cdot\left( ho_0 u hinspace\mathsf S ight), \] \[ ho_0 T_0\left(\partial_t s' + u_r rac{ds_0}{dr} ight) = abla\cdot\left(\kappa hinspace ho_0 T_0 abla s' ight), \]

with the reduced pressure \(\Pi = p'/ ho_0 + \Phi'\) (\(\Phi'\) the perturbation of the gravitational potential) and the rate-of-strain tensor without its trace,

\[ \mathsf S = abla\mathbf u + ( abla\mathbf u)^{\mathsf T} - frac{2}{3}( abla\cdot\mathbf u) hinspace\mathsf I . \]

The momentum equation is per unit mass. The flow is not solenoidal: \( abla\cdot\mathbf u = -u_r hinspace d\ln ho_0/dr\). The viscous force is the divergence of the full stress \( ho_0 u hinspace\mathsf S\), with the terms that come from \(d\ln ho_0/dr\), from \(d u/dr\) and from \( abla\cdot\mathbf u\). Any \( u(r)\) is allowed. The bulk viscosity is zero. The heat flux is a diffusion of entropy.

What is dropped. Starting from the linearised compressible equations about the same background, LBR drops two things (Brown et al. 2012; Vasil et al. 2013):

  1. The acoustic part of \(\partial_t ho'\) in the mass equation. This removes sound.
  2. The entropy part of \(\partial_t ho'\) in the mass equation, together with the force \((N^2/g)(p'/ ho_0) hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\) in the momentum equation. That force is the buoyancy of the density \(p'/c^2\) that the pressure perturbation induces, in the part of the stratification that is not adiabatic. These two terms must be dropped together.

The second step treats the background as adiabatic wherever the entropy gradient only corrects a term that is already there. The entropy gradient is kept in the heat equation, where it is the source of \(s'\) and gives gravity waves their restoring force. The Coriolis force, the self-gravity (absorbed into \(\Pi\)) and the viscous force are not approximated.

Energy. Multiply the momentum equation by \( ho_0\mathbf u^*\) and integrate. The pressure does no work, although \( abla\cdot\mathbf u eq 0\), because \( abla\Pi\) is a gradient acting on the solenoidal \( ho_0\mathbf u\) and \(u_r = 0\) on the walls. The Coriolis force does no work, and the viscous force only dissipates, \(- frac12\int ho_0 u hinspace\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV \le 0\), for any \( u(r)\). This holds only because the two terms of item 2 are dropped together: an anelastic set that keeps the force but drops the mass term makes the pressure do work (Brown et al. 2012).

docs.title: Non-dimensionalization
docs.text:
kore assumes \(\alpha T_0 = 1\) and uses \(p_0\) in place of \( ho_0 T_0\), both exact for an ideal gas of uniform composition. Each quantity is then a scale times a dimensionless variable:

quantity scale dimensionless variable length \(L\), the radius of the outer wall (r_out star radii) \(r\), with \(r = 1\) at the outer wall time \( au\) \(t\) velocity \(L/ au\) \(\mathbf u\) reduced pressure \(L^2/ au^2\) \(\Pi\) entropy perturbation and background entropy \(c_p\) \(s\), \(S\) gravity \(g_{\mathrm{ref}}\) the profile \(g(r)\) of the structure viscosity and thermal diffusivity \( u_{\mathrm{ref}}\), \(\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}\) the profiles \( u(r)\), \(\kappa(r)\) of diffusivity density and pressure any \( ho_0\), \(p_0\)

The equations are linear in \(\mathbf u\) and \(s\), and contain \( ho_0\) only through \(d\ln ho_0/dr\) and \(p_0\) only through its shape, so the scales of the velocity, of \( ho_0\) and of \(p_0\) do not matter. The solar structures have \(g = 1\) at the surface, so that \(g_{\mathrm{ref}}\) is the surface gravity; \( u_{\mathrm{ref}}\) and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}\) are the values where the diffusivity profiles are 1 (the convection zone for 'solar_rz' and 'step').

Insert these in the equations, multiply the momentum equation by \( au^2/L\) and the heat equation by \( au/c_p\):

\[ abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf u) = 0, \] \[ \partial_t\mathbf u + 2 hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u = - abla\Pi + \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace s hinspace\hat{\mathbf r} + \mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace rac{1}{ ho_0} abla\cdot\left( ho_0 u hinspace\mathsf S ight), \] \[ p_0\left(\partial_t s + u_r rac{dS}{dr} ight) = \mathrm{ThermaD} hinspace abla\cdot\left(\kappa hinspace p_0 abla s ight). \]

These are the equations kore solves. \(dS/dr\) is the background entropy gradient over \(c_p\), and \(g\), \( u\) and \(\kappa\) are dimensionless profiles, set by the parameters structure, stratification and diffusivity (Background model). Four numbers carry the scales:

parameter definition meaning Gaspard \(\Omega au\) rotation rate of the frame Beyonce \(g_{\mathrm{ref}} hinspace au^2/L\) gravity ViscosD \( u_{\mathrm{ref}} hinspace au/L^2\) viscosity; the Ekman number when \( au = 1/\Omega\) ThermaD \(\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}} hinspace au/L^2\) thermal diffusivity

The buoyancy frequency is

\[ N^2 = \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace rac{dS}{dr} \]

in units of \(1/ au^2\).

Eigenvalues. Fields go as \(e^{im\phi + \lambda t}\), with \(\lambda = \sigma - i\omega\): \(\sigma\) is the growth rate and \(\omega\) the frequency, in units of \(1/ au\) in the rotating frame; \(\omega > 0\) is prograde. Forced runs (forcing > 0) solve at \(\lambda = i hinspace\)forcing_frequency.

docs.title: The time scale
docs.text:
par.timescale and par.set_scales() set the four parameters from the Ekman number Ek \(= u_{\mathrm{ref}}/(\Omega L^2)\) and Etherm \(= \kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}/(\Omega L^2)\):

timescale \( au\) Gaspard ViscosD ThermaD Beyonce 'rotation' \(1/\Omega\) 1 Ek Etherm 0 'viscous' \(L^2/ u_{\mathrm{ref}}\) 1/Ek 1 Etherm/Ek 0 'free fall' \(\sqrt{L/g_{\mathrm{ref}}}\) 0 0 0 1

set_scales() resets all four, so set the ones it leaves at 0 after calling it (Beyonce with 'rotation'). The parameter files of this branch use 'rotation', and bin/units.py sets the parameters from physical values for that choice (Background model).

Ratios of the parameters do not depend on \( au\):

  • the Ekman number \(E = \mathrm{ViscosD}/\mathrm{Gaspard} = u_{\mathrm{ref}}/(\Omega L^2)\);
  • the Prandtl number \(Pr = \mathrm{ViscosD}/\mathrm{ThermaD} = u_{\mathrm{ref}}/\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}\);
  • the buoyancy frequency over the rotation rate, \(N/\Omega = \sqrt{\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace dS/dr} hinspace/\mathrm{Gaspard}\);
  • for convection, the Rayleigh number of an entropy drop \(\Delta S\) across the shell (inner minus outer wall), \(Ra = \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace\Delta S/(\mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace\mathrm{ThermaD}) = g_{\mathrm{ref}}L^3\Delta S/( u_{\mathrm{ref}}\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}})\);
  • the frequency over the rotation rate, \(\omega/\Omega = -\mathrm{Im} hinspace\lambda/\mathrm{Gaspard}\).

docs.title: The Boussinesq case
docs.text: With structure = 'Boussinesq' (\( ho_0 = p_0 = 1\), \(g = r\)) and diffusivity = 'uniform', the equations are the Boussinesq equations: \( abla\cdot\mathbf u = 0\), the viscous force is \(\mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace abla^2\mathbf u\), the diffusion is \(\mathrm{ThermaD} hinspace abla^2 s\), and the buoyancy is \(\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace r hinspace s hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\), with \(s\) in place of the temperature perturbation. With stratification 'linear' (\(dS/dr = r\)), \(N^2 = \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace r^2\).

docs.title: Without thermal diffusion
docs.text:
With ThermaD = 0 the heat equation loses its diffusion term,

\[ p_0\left(\partial_t s + u_r\frac{dS}{dr}\right) = 0 : \]

the entropy perturbation is only carried by the flow, and the motion is adiabatic. This is the limit for modes whose periods are short compared with the time of thermal diffusion. The equation is then first order in \(r\), so it takes no thermal boundary conditions: bci_thermal and bco_thermal are not used. The rows kore builds in that case are on Numerical method, and what to watch for in such runs is in Background model.

docs.title: Differential rotation
docs.text:
With a differential rotation \(\Omega(r,\theta) = \Omega_{\rm ref}\left[1 + \Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\right]\), kore solves in the frame rotating at \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\), where the background is a steady azimuthal flow,

\[ \mathbf{U}_0 = \mathrm{Gaspard}\thinspace\Delta\Omega\thinspace r\sin\theta\thinspace\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\phi . \]

The perturbation is advected and sheared by this flow. In the momentum equation this adds

\[ \mathrm{Gaspard}\left[\Delta\Omega\thinspace (i\thinspace m\thinspace \mathbf{u} + 2\hat{\mathbf{z}}\times\mathbf{u}) + r\sin\theta\thinspace (\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\Delta\Omega)\thinspace \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\phi\right] \]

to the left side: the advection by the local rotation and its Coriolis force, and the transport of angular momentum by the perturbation across the shear. The heat equation gains, inside the bracket multiplied by \(p_0\),

\[ i\thinspace m\thinspace\mathrm{Gaspard}\thinspace\Delta\Omega\thinspace s + u_r\thinspace \frac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial r} + \frac{u_\theta}{r}\thinspace \frac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial\theta}. \]

The first term is the advection of \(s\) by \(\mathbf U_0\). The other two are the advection, by the perturbation, of a latitudinal background entropy \(S_{tw}(r,\theta)\): either the thermal wind that balances \(\Omega(r,\theta)\) (the latitudinal entropy a differentially rotating star needs to be in equilibrium; Bekki, Cameron & Gizon 2022) or prescribed. In a convection zone these terms act at the same order as the momentum terms. The background is fixed: nothing maintains or evolves \(\Omega\) and \(S_{tw}\) against diffusion, and \(\rho_0\), \(T_0\) and \(g\) stay spherical (no centrifugal distortion). Differential rotation derives these terms and their spectral form.

docs.title: Where the approximation holds
docs.text:
• Sound-proof: \(\max(\lvert\lambda\rvert^2, 4\Omega^2) \ll c^2k^2\) for a mode of wavenumber \(k\), with \(c\) the sound speed. It fails for p modes and near a surface where \(c\to 0\).
  • Nearly adiabatic over the scale \(\ell\) of the motion: \(N^2\ell/g \ll 1\), the relative size of the dropped terms of item 2. In kore's units this is \(\lvert dS/dr\rvert\thinspace\ell \ll 1\). Their effect on frequencies is smaller, and for \(N \gg \omega\) it does not grow with \(N\), so a strongly stratified radiative zone is not a problem in itself. The case where it fails is that of low-order g modes with frequencies near \(N\).
  • A possible background: hydrostatic, and with \(N^2 < g/H_\rho\) (\(H_\rho\) the density scale height), since \(g/c^2 = -d\ln\rho_0/dr - N^2/g\) must be positive. In kore's units this is \(dS/dr < -d\ln\rho_0/dr\). kore never uses \(c\), so it cannot detect a background that breaks this: check it when choosing structure and stratification separately.

docs.title: Background model
docs.text:
kore solves for small perturbations of a background. The background has four parts, each chosen by name in the parameter file:

part parameter what it sets structure structure the density \(\rho_0\), \(p_0 = \rho_0 T_0\) and gravity \(g\), functions of \(r\) stratification stratification the entropy gradient \(dS/dr\), with \(S = \delta s/c_p\) (only with thermal = 1) diffusivity diffusivity the radial profiles of the viscosity \(\nu\) and the thermal diffusivity \(\kappa\) rotation diff_rot, diff_rot_type a uniform or a differential rotation \(\Omega(r,\theta)\), and the latitudinal entropy that balances it

The equations in which they enter are on the page Anelastic equations. The code is in bin/background.py (the choice, the checks, the stratification and diffusivity types), bin/radial_profiles.py (one class per structure) and bin/diff_rot.py (the rotation).

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
kore is dimensionless (Non-dimensionalization). The unit of length is the radius of the outer wall, \(r = 1\). r_out is that radius in star radii (1 by default), so \(x = r\cdot\)r_out is the radius in star radii, the coordinate of the solar profiles below. The only physical unit kore reads is that of the solar rotation data, in nHz.

bin/units.py turns physical values into the parameters, with the time unit \(1/\Omega\); kore itself never imports it. In a parameter file, after r_out is set:

import units
units.set_physical(par, frame_nHz=456.0, nu=1e12, kappa=1e12)   # Gaspard, Beyonce, ViscosD, ThermaD, diff_rot_frame
units.set_target(par, omega=-271.2, sigma=-33.2)                 # itau, rtau from ω, σ in nHz

set_physical takes \(\nu\) and \(\kappa\) in cm²/s and uses the solar radius and surface gravity unless radius and gsurf (cgs) are given. For the Sun with r_out = 0.985 in a frame rotating at 456 nHz it gives Beyonce \(= 4.86\times10^4\) and, for \(\nu = 10^{12}\) cm²/s, ViscosD \(= 7.4\times10^{-5}\). In a run directory, python3 bin/units.py prints the eigenvalues as \(\omega\) and \(\sigma\) in nHz, \(\omega = -\mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda\cdot F/\mathrm{Gaspard}\) and \(\sigma = \mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\cdot F/\mathrm{Gaspard}\), with \(F\) = diff_rot_frame the frame rate in nHz.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
The background of the smooth Sun example (examples/smooth_sun/parameters.py), a full sphere with the observed solar rotation:

par.thermal        = 1
par.r_out          = 0.985                 # outer wall in solar radii
par.structure      = 'model S hydrostatic'
par.stratification = 'solar_rz'            # a radiative interior below a slightly subadiabatic convection zone
par.solar_rz_delta_cz = -4e-7
par.diffusivity    = 'solar_rz'            # ν, κ drop to visc0, therm0 below 0.70 R☉
par.visc0, par.therm0 = 0.01, 0.04
par.diff_rot       = 1
par.diff_rot_type  = 'tabulated'           # Ω(r, θ) from a table
par.diff_rot_file  = 'bin/jsoc_hmi_2010_2026.npz'
par.diff_rot_nmax  = 4
par.thermal_wind   = 2                     # with its exact thermal wind
par.thermal_wind_radial = 0
units.set_physical(par, frame_nHz=456.0, nu=1e12, kappa=1e12)

The checked-in bin/parameters.py, a gravito-inertial mode, uses structure = 'Wu 2005' with r_out = 0.99 and stratification = 'top hat', with uniform rotation. Getting started uses an incompressible fluid ('Boussinesq', thermal = 0) with a shellular rotation.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
structure has no default.

structure \(\rho_0\), \(p_0\), \(g\) parameters 'model S hydrostatic' the Sun, for new runs: an even polynomial fit of \(\ln\rho\) of Model S (bin/model_s.at) over the whole Sun, \(g\) from its mass, \(p_0\) from hydrostatic balance structure_deg (30) 'Wu 2005' \(\rho_0 = (1 - x^2)^2\) (Wu 2005, \(\beta = 2\)) with its \(g\) and \(p_0\) r_out < 1, so that \(\rho_0 > 0\) at the wall 'Boussinesq' \(\rho_0 = p_0 = 1\), \(g = r\): the Boussinesq equations – '8-term fit' (legacy) the smooth fit of bin/smoothed_sun.py, up to 48 % off Model S in \(\rho\) near the surface, which moves solar inertial modes by 1.5–8 nHz – 'old model S prototype' (legacy) Chebyshev fits of \(\ln\rho\) and \(\ln p\) of Model S, with the \(g\) of the 8-term fit (not hydrostatic) solar_density_deg, solar_density_window, solar_density_sun_deg
  • Only ratios of \(\rho_0\) and of \(p_0\) enter the equations, so their scale does not matter. \(g\) is 1 at the surface (\(x = 1\)) in the solar structures and in 'Wu 2005'.
  • The three solar structures (the first and the last two rows) also make \(x = r\cdot\)r_out the radius of the solar rotation profiles (diff_rot.solar_x).
  • 'model S hydrostatic' is within 1.0 %, 0.5 % and 0.75 % of Model S in \(\rho\), \(p\) and \(g\) at degree 30, and within 0.14 %, 0.06 % and 0.10 % at degree 50. Use 50 to compare with papers that use Model S itself; degrees of 40 and above need about 16 more lmax for the same \(\ell\)-convergence of the HFR modes.
  • The two legacy structures are kept so that runs made before 'model S hydrostatic' give the same results. For 'old model S prototype', solar_density_window None fits the shell \([\)ricb\(\cdot\)r_out \(- 0.01\), r_out \(+ 0.005]\) when ricb > 0, and is 'sun' when ricb = 0: one even fit over the whole Sun of degree solar_density_sun_deg (60).

docs.title: Stratification
docs.text:
With thermal = 1, stratification sets \(dS/dr\) for \(r \ge 0\), in units of \(1/L\); it has no default then. In a full sphere (ricb = 0) kore uses it as an odd function of \(r\), so it should go to zero smoothly at the centre.

stratification \(dS/dr\) parameters 'top hat' \(\tfrac{A}{2}\left[\mathrm{erf}\frac{r - x_1}{w_1} - \mathrm{erf}\frac{r - x_2}{w_2}\right]\) aux1…aux5 = \(x_1\), \(w_1\), \(x_2\), \(w_2\), \(A\) 'odd top hat' the same made odd in \(r\): with \(x_1 = 0\) it rises as \(A\thinspace\mathrm{erf}(r/w_1)\) from the centre aux1…aux5 'solar_rz' the radiative interior of Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b, below solar_rz_dSdr, solar_rz_steps, solar_rz_core, solar_rz_delta_cz, solar_rz_delta_sf, solar_rz_os 'linear' \(r\); with 'Boussinesq', \(N^2\) = Beyonce \(r^2\) (Rieutord 2006, Mirouh et al. 2016) – 'inverse square' \(1/r^2\), conduction between the walls needs ricb > 0 'user' stratification_profile, a numpy expression (below) stratification_param (\(p\))
  • 'top hat' in a full sphere needs \(x_1 \gtrsim 6 w_1\), so that \(dS/dr \to 0\) at the centre; otherwise use 'odd top hat'. With ricb > 0 and ThermaD = 0, a \(dS/dr \neq 0\) at the inner wall gives spurious modes trapped there (below).
  • 'odd top hat' with aux1…aux5 = 0, 0.03, 0.68, 0.06, 2.6 fits the \(dS/dr\) of Model S to 10 % rms.

'solar_rz'. With \(x = r\cdot\)r_out in solar radii (their eq. 10, plus the convection zone of Bekki et al. 2024, eq. 2):

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{dS}{dr} &= \frac{A}{4}\left[1 - \mathrm{erf}\frac{x - x_1}{d}\right]\left[1 - \mathrm{erf}\frac{x - x_2}{d}\right]\mathrm{erf}\frac{x}{w_0}\cr &\quad + \delta(x)\thinspace \frac{d\ln p_0}{dr}\thinspace \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + \mathrm{erf}\frac{x - x_{OS}}{d_{OS}}\right], \end{aligned} \] \[ \delta(x) = \delta_{cz} + (\delta_{sf} - \delta_{cz})\thinspace e^{-((x - 0.985)/0.015)^2}, \]

with \(A\) = solar_rz_dSdr (2.615), \([x_1, x_2, d]\) = solar_rz_steps ([0.61, 0.68, 0.04]), \(w_0\) = solar_rz_core (0.05: makes \(dS/dr\) odd and smooth at \(r = 0\), no effect above \(x \approx 3w_0\)), \([x_{OS}, d_{OS}]\) = solar_rz_os ([0.70, 0.04]) and \(\delta_{cz}\), \(\delta_{sf}\) = solar_rz_delta_cz, solar_rz_delta_sf (0). \(A\) is their \((\partial s_0/\partial r)_{RZ}\) = 1.32e-2 erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹ cm⁻¹ times \(L/c_p\), with \(c_p\) = 3.46e8 and r_out = 0.985, so it scales with r_out. \(\delta < 0\) is subadiabatic; kore stops if \(\delta\) is set with another stratification. In the smooth Sun example, \(\delta_{cz} = -4\times10^{-7}\) makes the HFR \(m = 8\) mode 34 nHz more retrograde than \(\delta_{cz} = 0\).

docs.title: Diffusivity
docs.text:
\( u\) = ViscosD \(\hat u(r)\) and \(\kappa\) = ThermaD \(\hat\kappa(r)\); diffusivity sets \(\hat u\) and \(\hat\kappa\).

diffusivity \(\hat u\), \(\hat\kappa\) parameters 'uniform' (default) 1 – 'step' visc0, therm0 below \(r\) = aux3, 1 above, joined by an erf of width aux4 visc0, therm0, aux3, aux4 'solar_rz' visc0, therm0 below \(x_{OS}\), 1 above, as \( frac12[1 + \mathrm{erf}((x - x_{OS})/d_{OS})]\) (Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b, eqs. 8–9) visc0, therm0, solar_rz_os 'user' diffusivity_profiles = {'nu': '...', 'kappa': '...'}, numpy expressions (below) diffusivity_param (\(p\))
  • With 'step' and 'solar_rz', ViscosD and ThermaD are the values above the step (the convection zone of the Sun). Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b use visc0 = 0.01 and therm0 = 0.04.
  • Any type is multiplied by \(( ho_0(x_2)/ ho_0)^p\), \(x_2\) = aux3, with \(p\) = visc_pow for \(\hat u\) and therm_pow for \(\hat\kappa\): 0 (the default) keeps the kinematic diffusivities as set, 1 makes \( ho_0 u\) and \( ho_0\kappa\) follow the profile instead.
  • Forcing 11 (random Reynolds stresses) uses the turbulent part of the viscosity, ViscosD \((\hat u - u_f)\): the floor \( u_f\) is visc0 with 'step' and 'solar_rz' when visc0 < 1 and 0 otherwise, unless rsf_nu_floor is set.

docs.title: ThermaD = 0
docs.text:
ThermaD = 0 removes the thermal diffusion: the motion is adiabatic, and bci_thermal, bco_thermal are not used (Without thermal diffusion). It works with every structure, stratification and rotation option. What to watch for:

  • Prefer ThermaD = 0 to a very small ThermaD. As ThermaD → 0 the eigenvalues of a resolved diffusive run approach the ThermaD = 0 ones linearly. With the thermal wind and walls that are both stress-free and at fixed entropy (bci_thermal = bco_thermal = 0), a small ThermaD forms a thermal boundary layer of width about \((\mathrm{ThermaD}/\lvert\lambda\rvert)^{1/2}\) at the walls, which below ThermaD ≈ \(10^{-7}\) needs far more radial resolution than the bulk. The ThermaD = 0 run has no such layer, and neither have zero-flux or no-slip walls.
  • Let \(dS/dr\) vanish at the inner wall. In a shell, a \(dS/dr \neq 0\) at the inner wall gives spurious modes trapped there. Their eigenvalues move with N, and spin_doctor flags them (residσ ≈ 1). For an erf top hat, take \(x_1 \ge\) ricb \(+ 3w_1\). If the gradient must reach the wall, raise nev by one or two, because the spurious modes take some of the slots.
  • With a differential rotation, expect a band of eigenvalues near \(\sigma = 0\). Without diffusion, the advection of \(s\) by the rotation has a continuous spectrum, \(\lambda = -i\thinspace m\thinspace\mathrm{Gaspard}\thinspace\Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\), which the discretization shows as many eigenvalues near \(\sigma = 0\) with frequencies in the range of \(m\thinspace\mathrm{Gaspard}\thinspace\Delta\Omega\). With the thermal wind some of them grow slowly. They peak at \(l \approx\) lmax and change with lmax: discard any mode that fails the ℓ-convergence check of spin_doctor. They disappear with thermal_wind = 0 or with a moderate diffusivity (ThermaD ≈ \(10^{-3}\)). Put the target away from the band, where the solver converges slowly.
  • Check the convergence in N. In a full sphere, eigenfunctions with ThermaD = 0 need more radial resolution than diffusive ones (N = 200 instead of 120 for a smooth solar model). Where \(\rho_0\) nearly vanishes at the outer wall (structure 'Wu 2005' with r_out close to 1), the thermal-wind rows converge slowly in N.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
With diff_rot = 0 (the default) the background rotates uniformly at the rate of the frame. With diff_rot = 1 it rotates at

\[ \Omega(r,\theta) = \Omega_{\rm ref}\left[1 + \Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\right], \qquad \Delta\Omega = \sum_n f_n(r)\thinspace P_n(\cos\theta), \quad n = 0, 2, 4, \dots \]

where \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) is the rotation rate of the frame in which kore solves, and \(\Delta\Omega\) the relative departure from it, a sum of Legendre polynomials in \(\cos\theta\) with radial coefficients \(f_n(r)\). Only even \(n\) appear, so the rotation is symmetric about the equator. The profiles do not depend on the structure. With thermal = 1, the latitudinal entropy that balances the rotation, the thermal wind, is part of the background too (thermal_wind, below). The terms this adds to the equations are in Anelastic equations.

docs.title: Frame and units
docs.text:
\(\Delta\Omega\) is relative to the frame, and Gaspard converts it to the time unit, so any timescale works. Two things follow:

  • ViscosD, ThermaD and Beyonce must be computed for \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\). For 'solar' the frame must rotate at 435 nHz; for 'solar_P4' and 'tabulated' at diff_rot_frame (456 nHz by default). The other types are dimensionless.
  • With thermal_wind = 2 the eigenvalues do not depend on the choice of frame. With thermal_wind = 1 (linear in \(\Delta\Omega\)) they do, at second order in \(\Delta\Omega\): by 0.1–0.9 nHz for solar inertial modes.

Eigenvalues are in the frame rotating at \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\), as for uniform rotation.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: parameter default meaning diff_rot 0 1 adds the differential rotation diff_rot_type 'Y20' the profile, see below diff_rot_ampl 1.0 the factor of \(\Delta\Omega\), for every type (table below) diff_rot_param 0.0 the shape parameter: \(\sigma\) of 'shellular', p in 'user' expressions diff_rot_term_amp [1.0]*9 \(a_0, a_2, \dots, a_{16}\): factors of the \(P_0, P_2, \dots, P_{16}\) terms of \(\Delta\Omega\), any type, after diff_rot_ampl (missing entries are 1); e.g. [1, 1, 0] drops the \(P_4\) part of 'solar_P4' diff_rot_profiles {} 'user': {n: 'numpy expression'}, the shape \(f_n\) of each even degree (below) diff_rot_frame 456.0 'solar_P4', 'tabulated': \(\Omega_{\rm ref}/2\pi\) in nHz diff_rot_solar [464, -76, -50, 433.5, 0.71, 0.045] 'solar_P4': \(c_0\), \(c_2\), \(c_4\), \(\Omega_{RZ}\) (nHz), \(r_{tc}\), \(d_{tc}\) diff_rot_file '' 'tabulated': the .npz file, absolute or relative to the run directory diff_rot_nmax 8 'tabulated': highest degree kept, even (up to 16 with thermal_wind = 2) diff_rot_rdeg 24 'tabulated': degree of the Chebyshev fit of each \(f_n\) in \(r\) diff_rot_window None 'tabulated': None fits over the shell if ricb > 0 and is 'sun' if ricb = 0; 'sun': one fit over the whole Sun, even in \(r\), the same for any ricb diff_rot_sun_deg 60 'sun': degree of that fit thermal_wind 1 the latitudinal background entropy, see below thermal_wind_radial 1 0 drops \(u_r\thinspace \partial_r S_{tw}\) thermal_wind_amplitude 1.0 factor on \(S_{tw}\) (thermal_wind 1, 2) dSdtheta 0.0 thermal_wind = 3: \(\partial_\theta S_{tw}\) = dSdtheta \(\sin 2\theta\)

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
\(a\) = diff_rot_ampl, \(p\) = diff_rot_param. For the solar types \(x\) is the fractional solar radius: \(x = r\times\)r_out with a solar structure, \(x = r\) otherwise.

diff_rot_type \(\Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\) degrees notes 'rigid' \(a\) \(P_0\) test profile: a uniform offset of the rotation rate, with an exact answer (below); \(a = 0\) gives uniform rotation with the diff-rot machinery on (needed for thermal_wind = 3) 'Y20' \(a\thinspace P_2(\cos\theta)\) \(P_2\) \(P_2\) unnormalised, despite the name 'Y20-wall-bounded' \(a\thinspace (1 - r)(r - r_i)\thinspace P_2(\cos\theta)\), \(r_i\) = ricb \(P_2\) not smooth at \(r = 0\): use ricb > 0 'shellular' \(a\thinspace (r^\sigma - 1)\), \(\sigma = p\) \(P_0\) Baruteau & Rieutord 2013 (\(a = 1\)); not smooth at \(r = 0\) unless \(\sigma\) is even and positive 'shellular_boussinesq' \(\tfrac12 N_0^2\thinspace (1 - r^2)\), \(N_0^2 = a\) \(P_0\) Mirouh et al. 2016; use thermal_wind = 0 (their background has no thermal wind), structure 'Boussinesq' and stratification 'linear' 'cylindrical' \(\varepsilon\thinspace r^2\sin^2\theta\), \(\varepsilon = a\) \(P_0\), \(P_2\) Baruteau & Rieutord 2013; barotropic, \(S_{tw} = 0\) 'conical' \(\varepsilon\sin^2\theta\), \(\varepsilon = a\) \(P_0\), \(P_2\) Guenel et al. 2016 'solar' \(a\thinspace \times\) helioseismic fit, \(P_0 + P_2\), tanh step at \(x = 0.71\) of width 0.1 \(P_0\), \(P_2\) relative to 435 nHz; 4.5 nHz too fast at the equator and 12 nHz at the pole compared with the observations 'solar_P4' \(a\thinspace (\Omega/\Omega_{\rm ref} - 1)\), \(\Omega\) the fit below \(P_0\), \(P_2\), \(P_4\) diff_rot_solar, diff_rot_frame; defaults from Mukhopadhyay et al. 2026 'tabulated' \(a\thinspace (\Omega/\Omega_{\rm ref} - 1)\), \(\Omega\) from diff_rot_file \(P_0 \dots P_{n_{\max}}\) below 'user' \(a\sum_n f_n(r) P_n(\cos\theta)\), \(f_n\) from diff_rot_profiles the keys of diff_rot_profiles below

'rigid'. The eigenvalues are known exactly: with \(\lambda_0\) the diff_rot = 0 eigenvalue,

\[ \lambda(a, G) = \lambda_0\big(G(1 + a)\big) - i\thinspace m G a , \]

with \(G\) = Gaspard.

'solar_P4'. A rigid radiative zone joined by an erf step at the tachocline \(r_{tc}\) (width \(d_{tc}\)) to a convection zone whose rotation depends on latitude only:

\[ \frac{\Omega}{2\pi} = \Omega_{RZ} + \tfrac12\left[\Omega_{CZ}(\theta) - \Omega_{RZ}\right]\left[1 + \mathrm{erf}\thinspace \frac{x - r_{tc}}{d_{tc}}\right], \] \[ \Omega_{CZ} = c_0 + c_2\cos^2\theta + c_4\cos^4\theta , \]

with diff_rot_solar = [\(c_0\), \(c_2\), \(c_4\), \(\Omega_{RZ}\), \(r_{tc}\), \(d_{tc}\)] (nHz, and fractions of R☉).

'user'. diff_rot_profiles gives the shape of each even degree as a numpy expression (below). For example, the cylindrical rotation as a 'user' profile (it gives the same matrices as 'cylindrical'):

par.diff_rot_type     = 'user'
par.diff_rot_profiles = {0: '(2/3)*r**2', 2: '-(2/3)*r**2'}
par.diff_rot_ampl     = -0.25

The degrees must be even. Any degree up to 16 works with thermal_wind = 2 (32 with thermal_wind = 1).

'tabulated'. The file holds ome[θ, r] (nHz), r (R☉) and theta (rad), the layout of data/diff_rot.npz of the Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025 data set. tests/diff_rot/ls_to_tabulated.py converts the Larson & Schou 2018 table to it; bin/jsoc_hmi_2010_2026.npz is the mean of the 83 JSOC HMI 72-day inversions (hmi.V_sht_2drls, NACOEFF 36) from 2010-04-30 to 2026-06-29 in this layout, on the 151 table radii. kore projects \(\Omega\) on \(P_0 \dots P_{n_{\max}}\) at each table radius, fits each \(f_n\) in \(r\) over the table radii within 0.01 of the shell, and prints the fit residuals and the truncation error in nHz (the largest difference between the table and its expansion up to \(P_{n_{\max}}\)); check that line. For the Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025 profile the truncation error near the poles at the surface is up to 17 nHz at diff_rot_nmax = 8; 12 is the working choice.

docs.title: Thermal wind
docs.text:
With thermal = 1, thermal_wind chooses the latitudinal background entropy \(S_{tw}(r,\theta)\) and the terms the differential rotation adds to the heat equation. The advection of \(s\) by the rotation is always included.

thermal_wind heat-equation terms \(S_{tw}\) 0 the advection of \(s\) only none (e.g. Mirouh et al. 2016) 1 (default) and the advection of \(S_{tw}\) by the perturbation thermal wind of \(\Omega\) to first order in \(\Delta\Omega\) (\(S_{tw} \propto G^2/\)Beyonce) 2 the same thermal wind of the full \((1 + \Delta\Omega)^2\) balance; frame independent 3 the same prescribed: \(\partial_\theta S_{tw}\) = dSdtheta \(\sin 2\theta\), uniform in \(r\) (Bekki et al. 2024)
  • thermal_wind 1 and 2 need Beyonce > 0. With timescale = 'rotation', set_scales() sets Beyonce = 0, so set it after calling set_scales().
  • dSdtheta is in the units of \(s\) (\(\delta s/c_p\)): dSdtheta \(= \Delta_\theta s/c_p\), with \(\Delta_\theta s\) in erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Bekki et al. use \(c_p\) = 4.17e8, Model S has about 3.46e8. Negative values give warm poles. The thermal-wind amplitude does not apply.
  • thermal_wind_radial = 0 drops \(u_r\thinspace \partial_r S_{tw}\), as Bekki et al. 2022 and Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025 do. Keeping it is the consistent choice, but it moves the solar columnar and high-frequency retrograde modes by 5–15 nHz.
  • With the thermal wind \(S_{tw}\) is the only latitudinal entropy gradient; in a convection zone with \(dS_0/dr = 0\) it is also the only background entropy gradient, and its effect on the modes is of the same order as the momentum terms.
  • With diff_rot = 1 the default thermal_wind = 1 includes the thermal wind. For the advection of \(s\) by the rotation alone, set thermal_wind = 0.

docs.title: Resolution and cost
docs.text:
• A differential rotation couples harmonic degrees \(l\) that uniform rotation keeps apart, so the matrices get wider. Let \(n_{\max}\) be the highest degree of \(\Delta\Omega\). The momentum rows then couple degrees that differ by up to \(n_{\max}\) (\(P \to P\), \(T \to T\)) or \(n_{\max} + 1\) (\(P \leftrightarrow T\)).
  • \(S_{tw}\) has degrees up to \(n_{\max} + 2\) (thermal_wind 1) or \(2n_{\max} + 2\) (thermal_wind 2), and the heat rows couple degrees that far apart. Matrices are therefore widest with 'tabulated' and a large diff_rot_nmax.
  • With ricb = 0 (a full sphere) the profiles are evaluated at \(\lvert r\rvert\), to keep them smooth at the centre. 'Y20-wall-bounded' and 'shellular' (except even \(\sigma > 0\)) have a kink at \(r = 0\) and submatrices.py prints a WARNING. The 'solar' tachocline step needs N ≈ 400 at ricb = 0.
  • Modes that reach into a radiative interior have short radial wavelengths. In a full sphere with the radiative interior of stratification 'solar_rz', solar inertial modes needed N = 768 to 1024 for the spin_doctor residuals, although their eigenvalues converge at a lower N. Solver has the memory this takes.
  • Check convergence with spin_doctor as for any run; its residuals include the terms of the differential rotation.

docs.title: 'user' profiles
docs.text:
stratification_profile, the two diffusivity_profiles and the diff_rot_profiles are numpy expressions of r (the kore radius), x (\(r\cdot\)r_out with a solar structure, \(r\) otherwise) and p (stratification_param, diffusivity_param or diff_rot_param), with sin, cos, tan, arcsin, arccos, arctan, sinh, cosh, tanh, exp, log, log10, sqrt, abs, sign, pi, where, minimum, maximum, erf, erfc. For example:

par.stratification = 'user'
par.stratification_profile = '2.5*exp(-((r - 0.75)/0.06)**2)'      # dS/dr in 1/L for r >= 0
par.diffusivity = 'user'
par.diffusivity_profiles = {'nu': '0.01 + 0.99*0.5*(1 + tanh((x - 0.70)/0.015))', 'kappa': '1'}

kore evaluates them at \(\lvert r\rvert\), so in a full sphere \(dS/dr\) is odd and \(\hat\nu\), \(\hat\kappa\) and the \(f_n\) are even whatever the expression; for a profile that is smooth at the centre, \(dS/dr\) should still vanish there. The expressions must not contain #: spin_doctor writes them at the end of each params.dat row, after a #.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text: Before anything is built, kore stops on a background that cannot work: an unknown type, a parameter name of an older version of kore (the message gives the replacement), 'Wu 2005' without \(0 <\) r_out \(< 1\), 'inverse square' with ricb = 0, \(\delta\) without 'solar_rz', or a 'user' expression that does not evaluate. submatrices.py also warns about any name in the parameter file that kore does not define, so a misspelt name is not ignored without notice. spin_doctor records the background of every solution in params.dat (Output files).

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
kore reproduces published eigenvalues of differentially rotating fluids, from an incompressible fluid to the solar convection zone with a radiative interior. This page gives the set-up of each benchmark, the script that runs it, and the result.

benchmark physics result Baruteau & Rieutord 2013 incompressible, shellular and cylindrical rotation reproduced Guenel et al. 2016 incompressible, conical rotation reproduced, including an unstable mode Mirouh et al. 2016 Boussinesq, stably stratified, shellular rotation reproduced Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025a solar convection zone, observed rotation, thermal wind reproduced, including an unstable mode Bekki et al. 2024 onset of the high-latitude instability reproduced Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b solar convection zone with a radiative interior reproduced, except two high-latitude modes

The scripts are in tests/diff_rot/. Each one builds a run directory with a copy of bin/ and its own parameters.py, runs submatrices.py and assemble.py, and solves near the published eigenvalue. Getting started runs one of these benchmarks, fig. 10 of Baruteau & Rieutord, step by step.

Conventions. kore's eigenvalue is \(\lambda = \sigma - i\omega\) for fields \(\propto e^{\lambda t + im\phi}\) in the frame rotating at \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) (Anelastic equations). The three fluid-dynamics papers work in the inertial frame, with fields \(\propto e^{i\Omega_p t + im\phi}\) (Baruteau & Rieutord, Guenel et al.) or \(e^{(\tau + i\omega)t + im\phi}\) (Mirouh et al.), so their frequency is \(\mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda - m\) and their damping rate \(\tau = \mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\), in units of \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\). The solar papers give frequencies in nHz in the frame rotating at 456 nHz, negative for retrograde modes, and growth rates in nHz.

docs.title: Incompressible and Boussinesq fluids
docs.text:
These three papers use a viscous fluid in a spherical shell with stress-free walls. Their Ekman number is \(E = \nu/(\Omega_{\rm ref}R^2)\), which is ViscosD with timescale = 'rotation'. The common settings are

par.timescale = 'rotation'; par.set_scales()
par.structure = 'Boussinesq'                 # uniform density
par.bci = par.bco = 0                        # stress-free
par.diff_rot = 1; par.thermal_wind = 0
par.ricb = 0.35                              # their η, unless stated
par.ViscosD = 1e-8                           # their E

tests/diff_rot/lit_bench.py WORKDIR CASE builds and solves one published mode; lit_bench.py WORKDIR list prints the cases (br*, gu*, mi*). The runs take minutes on 8 ranks; the largest needs 26 GB.

docs.title: Baruteau & Rieutord 2013
docs.text:
JFM 719, 47. Shellular rotation \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}(r/R)^\sigma\), with \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) the surface rate, and cylindrical rotation \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}(1 + \varepsilon s^2)\), with \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) the rate on the axis:

par.thermal = 0
par.diff_rot_type = 'shellular';   par.diff_rot_param = -0.5   # σ: ΔΩ = r^σ - 1
par.diff_rot_type = 'cylindrical'; par.diff_rot_ampl = -0.4    # ε: ΔΩ = ε r² sin²θ

Result. For the 12 modes compared, the frequencies agree to \(2\times10^{-4}\thinspace\Omega_{\rm ref}\) and the damping rates to 1 %, once kore is resolved (some modes need more resolution than the paper used). Two modes differ in the damping rate: an \(m = 3\) mode in a cluster that does not settle with resolution, and the growing \(m = -6\) mode, whose growth rate is 6 % lower, a shift of 0.4 % in its critical Ekman number. Two modes at \(E \le 5\times10^{-9}\) need about 190 GB and were not computed.

docs.title: Guenel et al. 2016
docs.text:
A&A 589, A22. Conical rotation \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}(1 + \varepsilon\sin^2\theta)\), in the frame rotating at the pole:

par.thermal = 0
par.diff_rot_type = 'conical'; par.diff_rot_ampl = -0.25      # ε
par.ricb = 0.71

Result. For the 7 modes compared, the frequencies agree to \(10^{-4}\thinspace\Omega_{\rm ref}\) (\(5\times10^{-4}\) for one) and six damping or growth rates to 1 %, including the unstable mode with a corotation layer. The seventh, at \(\eta = 0.10\), sits in a cluster and is 6 % off in damping rate.

docs.title: Mirouh et al. 2016
docs.text:
JFM 800, 213. A stably stratified Boussinesq fluid with \(N^2\) uniform, \(g = r\), the temperature fixed at both walls, and the rotation \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}\left[1 + \tfrac{N^2}{2}(1 - r^2)\right]\):

par.thermal = 1; par.stratification = 'linear'               # dS/dr = r, so the buoyancy frequency is N² r² with g = r
par.bci_thermal = par.bco_thermal = 0
par.Beyonce = 1.5                                            # their N²
par.ThermaD = 1e-7                                           # their E/P
par.diff_rot_type = 'shellular_boussinesq'; par.diff_rot_ampl = 1.5   # N² again

thermal_wind = 0 is required: their background is balanced by centrifugal buoyancy, which kore does not carry.

Result. Of the 14 modes, 13 are identified. Their frequencies agree to \(2\times10^{-4}\thinspace\Omega_{\rm ref}\), and the damping or growth rates of 9 to 1 % and of 3 more to 2–4 %. One mode at \(E = 10^{-10}\) needs more resolution than fits in memory. A growing mode in a dense cluster of corotation modes is not identified.

docs.title: The Sun
docs.text: These papers solve the fully compressible equations about Model S; kore is anelastic. The common set-up: the Model S density, \(\nu = \kappa = 10^{12}\) cm² s⁻¹, an adiabatic convection zone, stress-free walls, the frame rotating at 456 nHz and their rotation profile. "With the thermal wind" means thermal_wind = 2 without \(u_r\thinspace\partial_r S_{tw}\) (thermal_wind_radial = 0), as in the papers.

docs.title: Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025a
docs.text:
A&A, arXiv 2501.16797. The convection zone, 0.71–0.985 R☉, with their tabulated rotation, the file data/diff_rot.npz of their data set (doi:10.17617/3.NP26AI):

import units
par.timescale = 'rotation'; par.set_scales()
par.structure = 'old model S prototype'                  # the Model S density
par.r_out = 0.985; par.ricb = 0.71/0.985
par.thermal = 1
par.stratification = 'odd top hat'                       # with aux5 = 0: dS/dr = 0
par.aux1, par.aux2, par.aux3, par.aux4, par.aux5 = 0.0, 0.1, 0.68, 0.06, 0.0
par.bci = par.bco = 0; par.bci_thermal = par.bco_thermal = 1
par.diff_rot = 1; par.diff_rot_type = 'tabulated'; par.diff_rot_file = 'diff_rot.npz'
par.diff_rot_nmax = 12
par.thermal_wind = 2; par.thermal_wind_radial = 0
units.set_physical(par, frame_nHz=456.0, nu=1e12, kappa=1e12)   # Gaspard, Beyonce, ViscosD, ThermaD, diff_rot_frame
par.N = 64; par.lmax = par.m + 63

tests/diff_rot/mk_bekki.py NAME m=… symm=… file=… builds this run for any \(m\) and symmetry, and solve_bekki.py NAME FREQ GROWTH solves it near a frequency and growth rate in nHz. run_bekki.py DIFF_ROT_NPZ runs the five modes below (about a minute each, one core).

Result. For the \(m = 3\) Rossby modes (\(n = 0, 1\)), the \(m = 3\) columnar mode, the \(m = 10\) high-frequency retrograde mode and the unstable \(m = 1\) high-latitude mode, kore agrees with their compressible values to 0.2 nHz in frequency and 0.4 nHz in growth rate. The high-latitude mode is at −95.76 nHz with growth rate +11.30 nHz (theirs: −95.70, +11.69). This needs the thermal wind: without it the frequencies are off by up to 11 nHz and the high-latitude mode is stable.

docs.title: Bekki et al. 2024
docs.text:
The high-latitude mode of the previous set-up becomes baroclinically unstable when the poles are warm enough. With thermal_wind = 3 the latitudinal entropy gradient is prescribed, \(\partial_\theta S_{tw}\) = dSdtheta \(\sin 2\theta\), with dSdtheta \(= \Delta_\theta s/c_p\) (negative: warm poles):

tests/diff_rot/mk_bekki.py RUN tw=3 ds=-1000 file=diff_rot.npz m=1 symm=-1
tests/diff_rot/solve_bekki.py RUN -93 5

with ds = \(\Delta_\theta s\) in erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Result. The \(m = 1\) high-latitude mode becomes unstable at \(\lvert\Delta_\theta s\rvert\) = 425 erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹ with the rotation of Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025, and at 546 with the Larson & Schou 2018 table, for \(c_p = 3.46\times10^{8}\). The published value is about 500. The radial shear of the rotation in the lower convection zone sets the onset: a rotation profile uniform in radius needs about four times more.

docs.title: Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b
docs.text:
A&A 708, A253. The convection zone extended down to 0.5 R☉ with their stably stratified, rigidly rotating radiative interior:

par.ricb = 0.5/0.985
par.solar_density_window = 'sun'                                # one Model S fit over the whole Sun
par.stratification = 'solar_rz'; par.diffusivity = 'solar_rz'   # their eqs. (8)-(10)
par.visc0, par.therm0 = 0.01, 0.04                              # ν and κ below 0.70 R☉, relative to the convection zone
par.diff_rot_type = 'solar_P4'                                  # their eqs. (5)-(6)
par.bci_thermal = 1; par.bco_thermal = 0                        # zero entropy flux at the bottom, s = 0 at the top
par.N = 128

the rest as above. tests/diff_rot/mk_rz.py NAME rin=0.5 m=… symm=… builds it for any inner radius rin (in R☉, 0 for the full sphere). tests/diff_rot/solar_checks.py DIFF_ROT_NPZ runs the modes of both Mukhopadhyay papers, with and without the thermal wind (about 40 minutes on one core).

Result. Without the thermal wind, every convection-zone and mixed mode whose counterpart can be identified (8 modes) agrees with theirs to 0.13 nHz, and the two published growth rates to 0.006 nHz. With the thermal wind the convection-zone modes are 2–10 nHz off, so their radiative-interior runs appear to have no latitudinal entropy gradient, unlike those of 2025a. Their two high-latitude convection-zone modes (\(m = 1\) and 2) are not matched: without the thermal wind kore's nearest convection-zone modes are strongly damped, and the paper gives no growth rates to compare.

docs.title: Differential rotation: equations and implementation
docs.text:
This page is the reference for the differential rotation: the physics, the equations, and how the code builds them. The parameters are on the page Background model, and the comparisons with published results on the page Benchmarks. It covers:

  • the physics: what a differentially rotating background does to a linear perturbation (§1);
  • the anelastic (LBR) equations with differential rotation, and the derivation of every term that the differential rotation adds to the momentum and heat equations (§2);
  • the spectral form of these terms: how they couple spherical-harmonic degrees, and how the angular coupling coefficients are obtained (§3);
  • the implementation, term by term: radial profiles, operator labels, the operators, the assembly of the matrices and the diagnostics (§4 to §8);
  • the tests of the implementation, and the known limitations (§9, §10).

Code references give the file and the function.

Contents

  • 0. Notation and code names
  • 1. Physics
  • 2. Equations
  • 3. Spectral form
  • 4. Implementation overview
  • 5. Radial profiles
  • 6. Radial operators and labels
  • 7. The operators and the assembly
  • 8. Diagnostics
  • 9. Tests
  • 10. Limitations

docs.title: 0. Notation and code names
docs.text:
Everything is dimensionless. The length unit is the outer radius \(r_0\) (r = 1 at the outer boundary), and the time unit is \(\tau\), chosen by par.timescale ('rotation' gives \(\tau = 1/\Omega_{\rm ref}\)).

symbol meaning in the code \(r, \theta, \phi\); \(x\) spherical coordinates; \(x = \cos\theta\) \(\varpi\) cylindrical radius \(r\sin\theta\) \(\hat{\mathbf z}\) rotation axis \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) rotation rate of the frame in which kore solves diff_rot_frame (nHz) for the solar profiles \(G\) \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\tau\), the frame's rotation rate in time units par.Gaspard \(\Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\) relative differential rotation, \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}(1 + \Delta\Omega)\) par.diff_rot_type \(f_n(r)\) Legendre coefficients of \(\Delta\Omega\): \(\Delta\Omega = \sum_n f_n(r) P_n(x)\), \(n\) even (diff_rot_ampl times \(a_n\) (diff_rot_term_amp) times the shape of the type) zf0, zf2, zf4, …; Two code conventions recur everywhere:

  • Sections. The unknowns and the matrix rows are stacked in blocks: section u holds the rows of the radial component of the double curl of the momentum equation (one row block per poloidal degree), section v the rows of the radial component of its curl (one per toroidal degree), and section h the heat equation (one per degree of \(s\), which follows the poloidal degrees).
  • Row weights. Each row is multiplied by a power of \(r\) and of \(\rho_0\), chosen so that every radial coefficient is a polynomial, and divided by \(L'^3\), where \(l'\) is the row degree.

docs.title: 1.1 The background
docs.text:
kore solves in a frame rotating at the constant rate \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\). The background rotates at

\[ \Omega(r,\theta) = \Omega_{\rm ref}\left[1 + \Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\right], \qquad \Delta\Omega = \sum_{n = 0, 2, 4, \dots} f_n(r) P_n(\cos\theta) . \]

Only even \(n\) appear, so the rotation is symmetric about the equator, and the equatorial symmetry of the modes (par.symm) still separates the problem into two classes. In the rotating frame the differential rotation is a steady azimuthal flow

\[ \mathbf U_0 = G\thinspace \Delta\Omega\thinspace r\sin\theta\thinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi = G\thinspace \Delta\Omega\thinspace \hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf r . \qquad (1.1) \]

The factor \(G\) = Gaspard converts the rotation rate \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\Delta\Omega\) to the time unit \(\tau\). It is 1 when \(\tau = 1/\Omega_{\rm ref}\). \(G\) does not choose the frame: \(\Delta\Omega\) is defined relative to the frame, and for the solar profiles the frame rate is set by diff_rot_frame (or fixed at 435 nHz for 'solar').

The spherical background (\(\rho_0\), \(T_0\), \(g\), \(S_0\), \(\nu\), \(\kappa\)) is the same as without differential rotation. The differential rotation adds only two things: the flow \(\mathbf U_0\), and a latitudinal entropy \(S_{tw}(r,\theta)\) (§1.3).

docs.title: 1.2 What the differential rotation does to a perturbation
docs.text:
A perturbation \(\mathbf u\) is carried by the background flow and sheared by it. Linearising the advection \((\mathbf U_0 + \mathbf u)\cdot\nabla(\mathbf U_0 + \mathbf u)\) gives (§2.3) three effects:

  1. Advection at the local rotation rate. A pattern \(e^{i m\phi}\) is carried round at the local rate \(G\Delta\Omega\), which shifts its frequency by \(-m G\Delta\Omega\) locally. With uniform \(\Delta\Omega\) this is just a Doppler shift.
  2. Coriolis force of the local rotation. The Coriolis parameter becomes \(2G(1 + \Delta\Omega)\) instead of \(2G\). Together with (1), a uniform \(\Delta\Omega\) is exactly a change of frame (§2.6).
  3. Transport across the shear. A perturbation that moves across the gradient of \(\Omega\) carries its angular momentum to a place where the background rotates at a different rate. This is the term \(r\sin\theta\thinspace (\mathbf u\cdot\nabla\Delta\Omega)\thinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi\). It is the only term through which the perturbation can exchange kinetic energy with the background flow (§2.3), so it is what drives shear instabilities.

In the heat equation the entropy perturbation is advected by \(\mathbf U_0\) (the same Doppler shift for \(s\)), and the perturbation velocity advects the latitudinal background entropy \(S_{tw}\).

docs.title: 1.3 Thermal-wind balance
docs.text:
A rotation rate that varies along the rotation axis cannot be balanced by pressure alone. The centrifugal force of the differential rotation then has a curl, and in a stratified fluid only a buoyancy force that varies with latitude, that is a latitudinal entropy gradient, can balance it. This is thermal-wind balance. A differentially rotating star in equilibrium therefore has a background entropy \(S_0(r) + S_{tw}(r,\theta)\). kore computes \(S_{tw}\) from \(\Delta\Omega\) (thermal_wind 1 or 2), prescribes it (thermal_wind = 3), or omits it (thermal_wind = 0).

\(S_{tw}\) is small in amplitude, since it scales as \(G^2/(\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g)\): for the Sun (Beyonce ≈ \(4.9\times10^4\)) its contrast from pole to equator is about \(5\times10^{-6}\) in units of \(c_p\), or \(2\times10^3\) erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹. But the buoyancy it produces through a perturbation scales as \(\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g\thinspace s\). The product does not depend on Beyonce: the feedback of \(S_{tw}\) on the motion is of order \(\Delta\Omega\) relative to the Coriolis force, the same order as the momentum terms of §1.2. In a convection zone, where \(S_0' \approx 0\), \(S_{tw}\) is the only background entropy gradient, and the meridional flow of a perturbation across it (the baroclinic coupling) can destabilise modes.

docs.title: 1.4 What is not modelled
docs.text:
• The background is imposed and fixed: nothing maintains \(\Omega\) or \(S_{tw}\) against viscosity or diffusion, and the perturbation equations have no source terms for them.
  • \(\rho_0\), \(T_0\) and \(g\) stay spherical: no centrifugal distortion, no latitudinal variation of \(\rho_0 T_0\) or \(g\) induced by the thermal wind, and no thermal-wind density in the mass flux. These effects are of relative size \(\Delta\Omega/(\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g)\).
  • The thermal wind is the one consistent with LBR buoyancy. The full anelastic balance would add a term \(p_b S_0'/(\rho_0 g)\) to \(S_{tw}\) (\(p_b\) the background pressure perturbation), the analogue of the \(p_1 S_0'\) term that LBR drops for the perturbations. It matters only where \(S_0' \neq 0\).
  • There is no magnetic field and no viscous heating.

docs.title: 2.1 The linear anelastic (LBR) equations
docs.text:
In the frame rotating at \(\Omega_{ m ref}\), with the background of §1.1, a perturbation \((\mathbf u, s)\) obeys, per unit mass (Lantz–Braginsky–Roberts form, with \(\varpi'\) the reduced pressure \(p'/ ho_0\)):

\[ rac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial t} + 2G hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u + \mathbf W(\mathbf u) = - abla\varpi' + \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace s hinspace \hat{\mathbf r} + \mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace \mathbf F_ u(\mathbf u), \qquad (2.1) \] \[ abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf u) = 0, \qquad (2.2) \] \[ p_0\left[ rac{\partial s}{\partial t} + \mathbf U_0\cdot abla s + u_r S_0' + \mathbf u\cdot abla S_{tw} ight] = \mathrm{ThermaD} hinspace abla\cdot(\kappa hinspace p_0 abla s). \qquad (2.3) \]

Here \(\mathbf F_ u = ho_0^{-1} abla\cdot( ho_0 u hinspace \mathsf S)\) is the viscous force of the anelastic stress tensor \(\mathsf S\), and

\[ \mathbf W(\mathbf u) = (\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf u + (\mathbf u\cdot abla)\mathbf U_0 \qquad (2.4) \]

is the linearised advection by the background flow. Without differential rotation, \(\mathbf W = 0\), \(\mathbf U_0\cdot abla s = 0\) and \(S_{tw} = 0\), and (2.1)–(2.3) are kore's standard equations. The differential rotation adds exactly three terms: \(\mathbf W\) in (2.1), and \(p_0\mathbf U_0\cdot abla s\) and \(p_0\mathbf u\cdot abla S_{tw}\) in (2.3).

Remarks:

  • In LBR form the buoyancy depends on \(s\) only. The reduced pressure is a gradient, so it disappears when the curl of (2.1) is taken (§3.2): kore never solves for it.
  • The viscous force, the buoyancy and the diffusion are not changed by the differential rotation.
  • (2.2) is satisfied exactly by the poloidal–toroidal form of \(\mathbf u\) (§3.1).

kore solves the eigenvalue problem for fields \(\propto e^{\lambda t + i m\phi}\), so \(\partial_t o \lambda\) and \(\partial_\phi o i m\).

docs.title: 2.2 The background flow as a local rotation
docs.text:
Write the background rotation in time units as \(\Omega_d(r,\theta) = G\Delta\Omega\), so that \(\mathbf U_0 = \Omega_d\thinspace \hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf r\). Two identities are used below:

\[ \mathbf U_0\cdot\nabla = \Omega_d\thinspace \partial_\phi, \qquad (\mathbf v\cdot\nabla)(\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf r) = \hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf v , \]

for any vector \(\mathbf v\). In components, with \(\hat{\mathbf z} = \cos\theta\thinspace \hat{\mathbf r} - \sin\theta\thinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_\theta\),

\[ \hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf u = \left(-\sin\theta\thinspace u_\phi,\ -\cos\theta\thinspace u_\phi,\ \sin\theta\thinspace u_r + \cos\theta\thinspace u_\theta\right) \qquad (2.5) \]

in the \((\hat{\mathbf r}, \hat{\mathbf e}_\theta, \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi)\) basis.

docs.title: 2.3 Derivation of the momentum term
docs.text:
Advection of the perturbation by \(\mathbf U_0\). \((\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf u = \Omega_d hinspace \partial_\phi\mathbf u\), where \(\partial_\phi\) also acts on the unit vectors: \(\partial_\phi\hat{\mathbf r} = \sin heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi\), \(\partial_\phi\hat{\mathbf e}_ heta = \cos heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi\), \(\partial_\phi\hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi = -\sin heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf r} - \cos heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ heta\). With (2.5) this is

\[ (\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf u = \Omega_d\left[i m hinspace \mathbf u + \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u ight], \]

where \(i m hinspace \mathbf u\) means \(i m\) times each component.

Advection of \(\mathbf U_0\) by the perturbation.

\[ (\mathbf u\cdot abla)\mathbf U_0 = (\mathbf u\cdot abla\Omega_d) hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf r + \Omega_d hinspace (\mathbf u\cdot abla)(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf r) = r\sin heta hinspace (\mathbf u\cdot abla\Omega_d) hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi + \Omega_d hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u . \]

Sum. With \(\mathbf u\cdot abla\Delta\Omega = u_r\partial_r\Delta\Omega + (u_ heta/r)\partial_ heta\Delta\Omega\),

\[ \mathbf W = G\left[\Delta\Omega\left(i m hinspace \mathbf u + 2\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u ight) + \sin heta\left(r hinspace \partial_r\Delta\Omega hinspace u_r + \partial_ heta\Delta\Omega hinspace u_ heta ight)\hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi ight]. \qquad (2.6) \]

This is the force that operators.differential_rotation discretises. The three parts are those of §1.2: the Doppler term \(i m\Delta\Omega hinspace \mathbf u\); the Coriolis force of the local rotation \(2\Delta\Omega hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u\), which adds to the frame's \(2\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u\); and the shear term.

For \(\Delta\Omega = f(r)P_n(x)\), using \(\partial_ heta P_n(\cos heta) = -\sin heta hinspace P_n'(x)\), the components are

\[ egin{aligned} W_r/G &= f P_n\left[i m hinspace u_r - 2\sin heta hinspace u_\phi ight],\cr W_ heta/G &= f P_n\left[i m hinspace u_ heta - 2x hinspace u_\phi ight],\cr W_\phi/G &= f P_n\left[i m hinspace u_\phi + 2\sin heta hinspace u_r + 2x hinspace u_ heta ight]\cr &\quad + \sin heta\left[(r f') hinspace P_n hinspace u_r - f\sin heta hinspace P_n' hinspace u_ heta ight]. \end{aligned} \qquad (2.7) \]

The profile enters only as \(f\) and \(r f'\); the second derivative \(r^2 f''\) appears later, when the double curl differentiates \(W\) in \(r\) (§3.4).

Energy. For a mode, \(2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace \mathbf u^\ast\cdot\mathbf W hinspace dV\) is the rate at which \(\mathbf W\) removes kinetic energy. The Doppler part gives \(i m\int ho_0\Delta\Omega\lvert\mathbf u vert^2 dV\), which is imaginary. The Coriolis part gives \(\mathbf u^\ast\cdot(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u) = \hat{\mathbf z}\cdot(\mathbf u imes\mathbf u^\ast)\), which is also imaginary. Only the shear term, \(2G hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace r\sin heta hinspace u_\phi^\ast hinspace (\mathbf u\cdot abla\Delta\Omega) hinspace dV\), exchanges energy with the background. These parts shift the frequency (residω) or change the growth rate (residσ) in spin_doctor (§8).

docs.title: 2.4 Thermal-wind entropy
docs.text:
The balance. The steady background satisfies, in the rotating frame and per unit mass,

\[ (\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf U_0 + 2G hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf U_0 = - abla\varpi_b + \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace S_{tw} hinspace \hat{\mathbf r}, \]

where \(\varpi_b\) collects the pressure and gravity potential terms. With \(\mathbf U_0 = \Omega_d hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf r\), the left side is \(-(\Omega_d^2 + 2G\Omega_d) hinspace \varpi hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \varpi = -G^2\left[(1 + \Delta\Omega)^2 - 1 ight]\varpi hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \varpi\), the centrifugal and Coriolis forces of the differential rotation (\(\hat{\mathbf e}_ \varpi\) the cylindrical radial unit vector). The \(\phi\)-component of the curl removes \(\varpi_b\). Using \(( abla imes F\hat{\mathbf e}_ \varpi)_ \phi = \partial_z F\) and \(( abla imes F\hat{\mathbf r})_ \phi = -r^{-1}\partial_ heta F\),

\[ rac{1}{r} rac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial heta} = rac{G^2 hinspace r\sin heta}{\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g} hinspace rac{\partial (1 + \Delta\Omega)^2}{\partial z}, \qquad rac{\partial}{\partial z} = \cos heta hinspace rac{\partial}{\partial r} - rac{\sin heta}{r} rac{\partial}{\partial heta}. \qquad (2.8) \]

In the variable \(x\). With \(\partial_ heta = -\sin heta hinspace \partial_x\) and \(\partial_z = x\partial_r + r^{-1}(1 - x^2)\partial_x\), (2.8) becomes

\[ egin{gathered} rac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial x} = - rac{r^2 G^2}{\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g}\left[x hinspace rac{\partial F}{\partial r} + rac{1 - x^2}{r} rac{\partial F}{\partial x} ight], \qquad (2.9)\cr F = egin{cases} 2\Delta\Omega & ext{(linear)} \cr (1 + \Delta\Omega)^2 - 1 & ext{(exact)} \end{cases} \end{gathered} \]

thermal_wind = 1 uses the linear form, thermal_wind = 2 the exact one. Only the exact form is independent of the frame: \(G^2(1 + \Delta\Omega)^2\) is the square of the physical rotation rate, the same whatever \(\Omega_{ m ref}\) the profile is written against, whereas \(G^2\cdot 2\Delta\Omega\) is \(2\Omega_{ m ref}(\Omega - \Omega_{ m ref}) au^2\) and changes with the frame. With thermal_wind = 1 the modes therefore move with the choice of frame, at second order in \(\Delta\Omega\).

The right side of (2.9) is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \(n_{\max} + 1\) (linear) or \(2n_{\max} + 1\) (exact), so \(S_{tw} = \sum_n \sigma_n(r) P_n(x)\) has even degrees up to \(n_{\max} + 2\) or \(2n_{\max} + 2\). The \(l = 0\) part \(\sigma_0\) is a spherical entropy, absorbed in \(S_0\), and set to zero.

Closed forms for \(\Delta\Omega = f_0 + f_2 P_2\). Writing the bracket of (2.9) on \(P_1\) and \(P_3\) (with \(x P_2 = frac{3}{5}P_3 + frac{2}{5}P_1\), \(3x(1 - x^2) = frac{6}{5}(P_1 - P_3)\), \(P_2' = 3P_1\), \(P_4' = 7P_3 + 3P_1\)) and matching coefficients gives, with \(e = 0\) for thermal_wind = 1 and \(e = 1\) for thermal_wind = 2,

\[ egin{aligned} \sigma_2 &= - rac{2r^2G^2}{\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g}\Bigg[(1 + e f_0)\left( rac{f_0'}{3} + rac{f_2'}{21} + rac{4}{7} rac{f_2}{r} ight)\cr &\qquad + rac{e hinspace f_2 (f_0' + f_2')}{21}\Bigg],\cr \sigma_4 &= - rac{6r^2G^2}{35 hinspace \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g}\Bigg[(1 + e f_0)\left(f_2' - rac{2f_2}{r} ight)\cr &\qquad + e\left(f_2 f_0' + rac{4}{11}f_2 f_2' + rac{14}{11} rac{f_2^2}{r} ight)\Bigg],\cr \sigma_6 &= -e hinspace rac{4r^2G^2}{77 hinspace \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g} hinspace f_2\left(f_2' - rac{2f_2}{r} ight). \end{aligned} \qquad (2.10) \]

kore computes the \(\sigma_n\) from (2.9) by the Legendre-series algebra of §5.4, for any degrees of \(\Delta\Omega\); (2.10) is kept as a validation (tests/diff_rot/gen_check.py, §9). Two analytic checks:

  • Cylindrical rotation, \(\Delta\Omega = \varepsilon\varpi^2\), i.e. \(f_0 = frac{2}{3}\varepsilon r^2\), \(f_2 = - frac{2}{3}\varepsilon r^2\): \(\sigma_2 = \sigma_4 = \sigma_6 = 0\). A rotation constant on cylinders is barotropic and needs no thermal wind.
  • Conical rotation, \(\Delta\Omega = \varepsilon\sin^2 heta\), i.e. \(f_0 = frac{2}{3}\varepsilon\), \(f_2 = - frac{2}{3}\varepsilon\) (linear form): \(\sigma_2 = 16\varepsilon r/(21 hinspace\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g)\), \(\sigma_4 = -8\varepsilon r/(35 hinspace\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g)\), and \(S_{tw}( ext{pole}) - S_{tw}( ext{equator}) = \varepsilon r/(\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g)\): an equator rotating faster (\(\varepsilon > 0\)) needs warmer poles.

Prescribed latitudinal entropy (thermal_wind = 3). \(\partial_ heta S_{tw}\) = dSdtheta \(\sin 2 heta\), independent of \(\Omega\) and of \(r\). Since \(\sin 2 heta = - frac{2}{3} hinspace dP_2/d heta\),

\[ \sigma_2 = - frac{2}{3} hinspace exttt{dSdtheta}, \qquad \sigma_n = 0 \quad (n \ge 4). \]

dSdtheta is in the units of \(s\) (\(\delta s/c_p\)); negative values give warm poles. \(\Omega\) still enters through \(\mathbf W\) and the advection of \(s\). For a uniformly rotating background with a prescribed \(S_{tw}\), use diff_rot_type = 'rigid' with diff_rot_ampl = 0.

docs.title: 2.5 The heat-equation terms
docs.text:
\(S_{tw}\) does not depend on \(\phi\), so \(\mathbf U_0\cdot\nabla S_{tw} = 0\), and \(\mathbf U_0\cdot\nabla s = G\Delta\Omega\thinspace \partial_\phi s\). The left side of (2.3) gains

\[ p_0\left[\thinspace \underbrace{i m G\Delta\Omega\thinspace s}_ {\text{(a) advection}} + \underbrace{u_r\frac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial r}}_ {\text{(b) radial}} + \underbrace{\frac{u_\theta}{r}\frac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial\theta}}_ {\text{(c) latitudinal}}\thinspace \right]. \qquad (2.11) \]

(a) is always included. (b) and (c) are included for thermal_wind 1, 2, 3; thermal_wind_radial = 0 drops (b). (a) is anti-Hermitian under the entropy pairing \(\int s^\ast(\cdot)\thinspace dV\), so it only shifts the frequency; (b) and (c) exchange entropy variance with the flow.

docs.title: 2.6 An exact result: the rigid offset
docs.text:
For a uniform \(\Delta\Omega = a\) (diff_rot_type = 'rigid'), \(\partial\Delta\Omega = 0\), \(S_{tw} = 0\), and (2.6) and (2.11) reduce to \(G a(i m\mathbf u + 2\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf u)\) and \(i m G a\thinspace p_0 s\). Equations (2.1) and (2.3) become those of uniform rotation at rate \(G(1 + a)\), with \(\lambda\) replaced by \(\lambda + i m G a\). So

\[ \lambda(a, G) = \lambda_0\big(G(1 + a)\big) - i m G a , \qquad (2.12) \]

where \(\lambda_0(G)\) is the eigenvalue without differential rotation. This identity tests the Doppler and Coriolis parts of the operators and their signs (§9).

docs.title: 3.1 Fields
docs.text:
At fixed \(m\) and equatorial symmetry, each field is a sum over degrees,

\[ \mathbf u = \sum_l\left[ ho_0^{-1} abla imes abla imes( ho_0 P_l Y_l hinspace \mathbf r) + abla imes(T_l Y_l hinspace \mathbf r) ight], \qquad s = \sum_l s_l Y_l , \]

where \(P\) and \(s\) use the poloidal degrees and \(T\) the toroidal ones (utils.ell(m, lmax, symm) returns both lists). This form satisfies (2.2) exactly. For one degree, with \(Z_l = i m Y_l/\sin heta\) and

\[ a_l = rac{(r P_l)'}{r} + h' P_l = rac{P_l}{r} + P_l' + h' P_l , \qquad (3.1) \]

the components are

\[ u_r = rac{L P_l}{r} Y_l, \qquad u_ heta = a_l hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l + T_l Z_l, \qquad u_\phi = a_l Z_l - T_l hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l . \qquad (3.2) \]

These expressions underlie diff_rot._primitives (through the basis fields of §3.3), utils4pp.diff_rot_setup and ru_insane.py.

docs.title: 3.2 Projection of a vector field, and kore's rows
docs.text:
Any vector field \(\mathbf F\) is projected on vector spherical harmonics as

\[ egin{gathered} \mathbf F = \sum_l\left[F^q_l hinspace Y_l hinspace \hat{\mathbf r} + F^s_l hinspace r abla Y_l + F^t_l hinspace r abla Y_l imes\hat{\mathbf r} ight], \qquad (3.3)\cr r abla Y = \partial_ heta Y hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ heta + Z hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi, \qquad r abla Y imes\hat{\mathbf r} = Z hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ heta - \partial_ heta Y hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi , \end{gathered} \]

with, since \(\int(\lvert\partial_ heta Y_l vert^2 + \lvert Z_l vert^2) hinspace d\Omega = L n_l\),

\[ egin{aligned} F^q_l &= rac{1}{n_l}\int F_r Y_l^\ast hinspace d\Omega,\cr F^s_l &= rac{1}{L n_l}\int\left(F_ heta hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l^\ast + F_\phi Z_l^\ast ight)d\Omega,\cr F^t_l &= rac{1}{L n_l}\int\left(F_ heta Z_l^\ast - F_\phi hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l^\ast ight)d\Omega . \end{aligned} \qquad (3.4) \]

By (3.2) the velocity has \(u^q = L P/r\), \(u^s = a\), \(u^t = T\).

Taking curls removes the pressure:

\[ \hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes\mathbf F = \sum_l rac{L}{r}F^t_l Y_l, \qquad \hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes abla imes\mathbf F = \sum_l rac{L}{r^2}\left[F^q_l - \partial_r(r F^s_l) ight]Y_l . \qquad (3.5) \]

(The toroidal part \(F^t r abla Y imes\hat{\mathbf r} = abla imes(F^t Y\mathbf r)\) has no radial curl-curl, and the spheroidal part \(F^q Y\hat{\mathbf r} + F^s r abla Y\) has the curl \(r^{-1}\left[F^q - \partial_r(r F^s) ight] r abla Y imes\hat{\mathbf r}\).)

kore's rows of degree \(l'\) are (3.5) multiplied by \(r^{ m rpower} ho_0^{ m rhopower}\) and divided by \(L'^3\). With the defaults rpower_u = 5, rpower_v = 3, rhopower_u = rhopower_v = 1:

\[ \mathrm{row}_ u(\mathbf F) = rac{r^3 ho_0}{L'^2}\left[F^q_{l'} - \partial_r(r F^s_{l'}) ight], \qquad \mathrm{row}_ v(\mathbf F) = rac{r^2 ho_0}{L'^2}F^t_{l'} . \qquad (3.6) \]

For example, \(\mathbf F = \mathbf u\) gives \(\mathrm{row}_ u = \left[L r^2 ho_0 P - r^3 ho_0(2P' + rP'' + h'P + r h'' P + r h' P') ight]/L^2\) and \(\mathrm{row}_ v = r^2 ho_0 T/L^2\), which is operators.inertia. The diff-rot operator is (3.6) applied to \(\mathbf W\).

docs.title: 3.3 Angular primitives
docs.text:
Insert one source degree \(l\) of (3.2) into (2.7), with \(\Delta\Omega = f(r)P_n(x)\). Each component of \(\mathbf W\) is a sum of four radial "shapes" times angular functions:

shape radial factor from q \(f hinspace L P_l/r\) \(u_r\) with \(f\) a \(f hinspace a_l\) the consoidal part of \(u_ heta\), \(u_\phi\) T \(f hinspace T_l\) the toroidal part dq \((r f') hinspace L P_l/r\) \(u_r\) in the shear term

From (2.7) and (3.2), the angular functions, per unit \(G\) and per unit shape, are (\(Y = Y_l\), \(Z = Z_l\)):

Projecting each entry on the target degree \(l'\) with (3.4) defines twelve matrices \(C^k_{ m sh}[l', l]\), with \(k \in \lbrace q, s, t brace\) the projection and sh the shape. Then, for the target degree \(l'\),

\[ W^k_{l'} = G\sum_l\left[C^k_q hinspace f rac{L_l P_l}{r} + C^k_a hinspace f a_l + C^k_T hinspace f T_l + C^k_{dq} hinspace (r f') rac{L_l P_l}{r} ight]. \qquad (3.7) \]

The angular algebra. The \(C^k_{ m sh}\) are not computed by integration but built exactly, as sparse products of a few matrices on the degree index (bin/angular.py). Multiplying a field by a function of \(x\) maps degree \(l\) to a few neighbouring degrees, by two exact recurrences of the Schmidt harmonics (\(p_l\), \(q_l\) as in (3.8) below):

\[ egin{aligned} x hinspace Y_l &= p_l Y_{l+1} + q_l Y_{l-1} && o X,\cr (1 - x^2) rac{dY_l}{dx} = -\sin heta hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l &= (l+1)q_l Y_{l-1} - l p_l Y_{l+1} && o D , \end{aligned} \]

with rows the target degree and columns the source degree. Their adjoints under \(\int d\Omega\) (with \(N = \mathrm{diag}(n_l)\)) are \(X^\dagger = N^{-1}X^{ m T}N = X\) and \(D^\dagger = N^{-1}D^{ m T}N = 2X - D\) (integration by parts). \(P_n(X)\) and \(P_n'(X)\) follow from the three-term recurrences \((k+1)P_{k+1} = (2k+1)XP_k - kP_{k-1}\), \(P_{k+1}' = (k+1)P_k + XP_k'\). Write \(R_l = Y_l\hat{\mathbf r}\), \(S_l = r abla Y_l\), \(T_l = r abla Y_l imes\hat{\mathbf r}\) for the basis fields of (3.3), \(L\) for \(\mathrm{diag}(l(l+1))\) acting on the source and \(1/L'\) for the division of each row by its \(L'\) (0 for \(l' = 0\)). The operations needed by (2.7) are then:

operation result on \((q, s, t)\) from \(g(x) hinspace R_l\) \(q\): \(g(X)\) \(g(x) hinspace S_l\) \(s\): \((g(X)L - g'(X)D)/L'\), \(t\): \(-i m hinspace g'(X)/L'\) \(\int g abla Y_l\cdot abla Y_{l'}^\ast = \int Y_{l'}^\ast(L_l g Y_l - g' DY_l)\) \(g(x) hinspace T_l\) \(s\): \(i m hinspace g'(X)/L'\), \(t\): \((g(X)L - g'(X)D)/L'\) the same, rotated by \(\hat{\mathbf r} imes\) \(\hat{\mathbf z} imes(c hinspace Y\hat{\mathbf r})\) \(s\): \(-i m hinspace c/L'\), \(t\): \(D^\dagger c/L'\) \(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\hat{\mathbf r} = \sin heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi\) \(\hat{\mathbf z} imes S_l\) \(-i m R_l - x T_l\) (2.5) \(\hat{\mathbf z} imes T_l\) \(-(DY_l)\hat{\mathbf r} + x S_l\) (2.5) \(\sin heta hinspace F_ heta\) (a scalar) \(-D s + i m hinspace t\) \(\sin heta hinspace \partial_ heta Y = -DY\)

diff_rot._primitives composes them, per unit \(G\) and per unit shape:

\[ egin{aligned} \mathbf W_{ m sh} &= P_n(x)\left[i m hinspace \mathbf u_{ m sh} + 2\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u_{ m sh} ight] + \hat{\mathbf z} imes\left[-P_n'(x)\sin heta hinspace u_{ heta,{ m sh}} hinspace \hat{\mathbf r} ight],\cr \mathbf W_{dq} &= \hat{\mathbf z} imes\left[P_n(x) hinspace Y\hat{\mathbf r} ight], \end{aligned} \]

with \(\mathbf u_q = R_l\), \(\mathbf u_a = S_l\), \(\mathbf u_T = T_l\) (the second term, the \(u_ heta\) part of the shear term, vanishes for the shape q). Every product is a sparse product of banded matrices, so the cost is \(O(l_{\max})\) and the result is exact to round-off at any degree. The matrices are built up to \(l_w\) = lmax + n + 6, because a product of matrices truncated at \(l_w\) is wrong only in its last few degrees.

tests/diff_rot/quad_reference.py computes the same primitives by Gauss–Legendre quadrature of the table above, as an independent check (§9). That costs \(O(l_{\max}^3)\), and it fails from \(l = 646\) on, where scipy.special.sph_harm_y returns NaN.

docs.title: 3.4 From the primitives to the radial operators

Put (3.7) into (3.6) and expand \(a_l\) with (3.1). For the \(v\) rows this is direct:

\[ \mathrm{row}_ v(\mathbf W) = \frac{G r^2\rho_0}{L'^2}\left[(L_l C^t_q + C^t_a)\frac{fP}{r} + C^t_a\thinspace f(P' + h'P) + C^t_T\thinspace f T + L_l C^t_{dq}\frac{(rf')P}{r}\right]. \]

For the \(u\) rows, \(\partial_r(r W^s)\) differentiates the profile and the unknowns: with \(r a = P + rP' + r h' P\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_r(r f a) &= f'(P + rP' + rh'P) + f(2P' + rP'' + h'P + rh''P + rh'P'),\cr \partial_r\left(r\thinspace C_{dq}^s (rf')\frac{L_lP}{r}\right) &= L_l C^s_{dq}\left[(f' + r f'')P + (rf')P'\right], \end{aligned} \]
